documents.source: President Rutherford B. Hayes, proclamation, July 18, 1877. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The president’s own order; shows Washington calling strikers insurgents and sending troops.
documents.text: “I do hereby warn all persons engaged in or connected with said domestic violence and obstruction of the laws to disperse and retire peaceably to their respective abodes on or before 12 o’clock noon of the 19th day of July instant.”
documents.title: Hayes orders the strikers to disperse

documents.source: Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1, approved July 2, 1890. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The law itself; shows the tool courts later used against unions as combinations in restraint of trade.
documents.text: “Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is hereby declared to be illegal.”
documents.title: The Sherman Antitrust Act

documents.source: Statement of the Pullman Strikers, in Report on the Chicago Strike of June-July, 1894, U.S. Strike Commission (1895). Paraphrased.
documents.sourcing: The strikers’ own case, as heard by a federal commission; shows the grievance the government was asked to judge.
documents.text: Paraphrased from the strikers’ statement: the company cut wages by 20 to 30 percent during the depression but did not cut rents in the town it owned, and it refused to arbitrate the dispute, answering that it had nothing to arbitrate.
documents.title: The Pullman strikers state their case

documents.source: In re Debs, 158 U.S. 564 (1895). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The Supreme Court’s own words; shows the Court blessing troops against strikers.
documents.text: “If the emergency arises, the army of the Nation, and all its militia, are at the service of the Nation to compel obedience to its laws.”
documents.title: The Supreme Court on the army and the militia

documents.source: Photograph of Illinois National Guard troops outside the Arcade Building, Pullman, Chicago, 1894. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A photograph from the strike; shows armed troops deployed in the company town.
documents.title: Troops at Pullman

documents.source: “Promise and Performance” political cartoon on the Homestead strike, 1892. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A cartoonist’s view of Homestead; shows a locked-out mill under a rich owner.
documents.title: A cartoon of Homestead

documents.source: August Spies, address to the court, October 7, 1886, in The Chicago Martyrs (1899). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A condemned man’s own words; shows the courts sentencing labor radicals to death.
documents.text: “You may pronounce the sentence upon me, honorable judge, but let the world know that in A.D. 1886, in the State of Illinois, eight men were sentenced to death, because they believed in a better future; because they had not lost their faith in the ultimate victory of liberty and justice!”
documents.title: Spies on his sentence

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1865 and 1898 the federal government sided with business over labor to a large extent, sending troops, injunctions, and court rulings against strikers in every great conflict of the era, although its sympathy was not absolute, since federal commissions heard workers’ grievances and the law it wrote against trusts could in theory reach employers too.
Context: After the Civil War, railroads, steel, and oil grew into national businesses, and workers answered low pay and long hours with national unions and nationwide strikes.
Evidence: Document 1 shows the pattern starting in 1877, with President Hayes warning railroad strikers to disperse as insurgents. Document 3 shows the Pullman workers’ grievance: wages cut by 20 to 30 percent while rents stayed high, and a company that refused to arbitrate. Documents 4 and 5 show the answer: the Supreme Court placing the army and militia at the nation’s service, and armed troops in formation at Pullman.
Evidence continued: Document 6 shows the same pattern at Homestead, a locked-out mill under a rich owner. Document 2 shows the legal tool: the Sherman Act’s ban on combinations, which courts read against unions. Document 7 shows the harshest edge: eight men sentenced to death after Haymarket.
Outside evidence: At Homestead in 1892 the Pennsylvania governor sent 8,000 National Guard troops to retake Carnegie’s mill, and in 1894 President Cleveland sent federal troops to Chicago and jailed Eugene Debs for defying an injunction.
Complexity: the government was not simply a hired arm of business, since the Strike Commission heard the Pullman workers and the Sherman Act was written against trusts, but in every great strike the troops, the injunctions, and the verdicts fell on labor’s side of the line.
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the federal government sided with business over labor between 1865 and 1898.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for a thesis that makes a historically defensible claim about the extent to which the federal government sided with business over labor between 1865 and 1898, with a line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: A thesis that merely restates the prompt, or one that makes no claim about extent, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as post-Civil War industrialization, the growth of corporations, or the rise of national unions.
rubric.notEarned: A context that is only background on one document, or one set outside the period, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using the content of at least three documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using at least six documents to support the argument, with specific evidence from each.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without using their content, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for using at least one piece of specific outside evidence, such as the Great Railroad Strike of 1877, the Homestead lockout, or the AFL’s growth after 1886, to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Repeating document content without adding outside evidence does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for explaining how at least one document’s point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience matters to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying a document’s author without explaining why that matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Earns the point for a complex argument, such as showing that labor changed some parts of American life while leaving others unchanged, or that the same changes helped some Americans and hurt others.
rubric.notEarned: A one-sided argument that ignores counter-evidence, or a complexity move stated without support, does not earn the point.
